clinicalPearls: An abnormal arrangement of the aortic arch and its branches that encircles and compresses the trachea and oesophagus
Double aortic arch and right aortic arch with an aberrant left subclavian artery and left ligamentum are the commonest complete rings
Respiratory symptoms predominate, including stridor, a barking cough, wheeze and recurrent chest infections that may be mistaken for asthma
Oesophageal compression causes feeding difficulty, dysphagia and, in older children, dysphagia to solids
A pulmonary artery sling, in which the left pulmonary artery arises anomalously, compresses the trachea and is often associated with complete tracheal rings
Barium swallow showing posterior oesophageal indentation and cross-sectional angiography establish the diagnosis
Surgical division of the ring relieves compression, though tracheomalacia at the compressed segment may cause lingering symptoms
reference.pathophysiology: Vascular rings arise from abnormal regression or persistence of the paired embryonic aortic arches, producing vascular structures that completely or partially encircle the trachea and oesophagus. A double aortic arch forms a complete ring as both arches persist, while a right aortic arch with an aberrant left subclavian artery and a left arterial ligament completes a ring posteriorly. These structures exert extrinsic pressure on the airway and oesophagus, causing airflow obstruction, secondary tracheomalacia and impaired swallowing. A pulmonary artery sling, though strictly a partial ring, compresses the trachea as the anomalous left pulmonary artery courses between trachea and oesophagus and is frequently accompanied by complete cartilaginous tracheal rings that intrinsically narrow the airway.
additionalDifferentials: Tracheomalacia or laryngomalacia of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Barium oesophagram showing characteristic posterior indentation
CT or MR angiography to define the arch anatomy and ring components
Bronchoscopy to assess airway compression and associated tracheomalacia or complete tracheal rings
Echocardiography to detect associated intracardiac defects
Chest radiograph for arch sidedness and airway narrowing
Assessment for a pulmonary artery sling when tracheal narrowing is present
redFlags: Severe stridor or acute airway obstruction
Recurrent aspiration or life-threatening apnoeic episodes
Failure to thrive from significant feeding difficulty
Complete tracheal rings with a pulmonary artery sling causing critical airway narrowing
reference.prognosis: Surgical division of a symptomatic ring generally relieves compression with excellent long-term results, though residual tracheomalacia can cause persistent symptoms; associated complete tracheal rings carry higher risk.
pitfalls: Treating persistent stridor and wheeze as asthma and delaying diagnosis
Overlooking oesophageal compression as a cause of feeding difficulty
Failing to recognise an associated pulmonary artery sling and complete tracheal rings
Assuming surgery immediately resolves all symptoms when tracheomalacia persists
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
management: Divide symptomatic vascular rings surgically, dividing the lesser arch in a double aortic arch or the ligamentum arteriosum in a right arch with an aberrant left subclavian artery, to relieve tracheo-oesophageal compression
Reimplant the anomalous vessel for a pulmonary artery sling and address any coexisting complete tracheal rings with tracheoplasty
Observe asymptomatic rings found incidentally, with clinical follow-up
Support residual tracheomalacia and treat recurrent chest infections while the airway remodels
Define the anatomy preoperatively with CT or MR angiography, assess the airway with bronchoscopy and screen for associated cardiac defects by echocardiography
Manage through a multidisciplinary team of paediatric cardiothoracic surgery, airway or ENT specialists and cardiology
Follow up after repair for persistent airway symptoms arising from residual tracheomalacia
